# Exposition of Morita Contexts, Data, and Their Applications

## Overview

This paper presents a comprehensive treatment of generalized Morita contexts, introducing new theoretical frameworks that extend classical Morita theory to accommodate weaker forms of duality and equivalence between module categories. The work systematically develops the concepts of injective Morita contexts, Morita α-contexts, Morita semi-contexts, and Morita data, situating these constructions within a unified framework while highlighting their distinct applications.

## Injective Morita Contexts and Morita α-Contexts

The paper begins by providing a detailed exposition of **injective Morita contexts**, a class of Morita contexts distinguished by the property that the connecting bimodule morphisms—the maps that typically encode the trace ideals linking two rings in a classical Morita context—are required to be injective. This injectivity condition imposes a refined structural constraint that allows for a more nuanced analysis of the relationship between the associated module categories, going beyond the surjectivity conditions that characterize strict Morita equivalences.

Complementing this, the authors introduce and examine **Morita α-contexts**, in which the connecting bimodules are required to satisfy a local projectivity condition in the sense of Zimmermann-Huisgen. This notion of local projectivity, originally developed to handle situations where classical projectivity fails but a suitable approximation still holds, provides a flexible framework for extending Morita-type equivalences to settings where the bimodules involved do not possess full projectivity. The incorporation of this concept allows the paper to capture a broader class of ring and module relationships that arise naturally in non-classical settings.

## Morita Semi-Contexts and Morita Data

Motivated by the observation that many naturally occurring situations do not require the full symmetric structure of a classical Morita context, the authors introduce two new organizing concepts: **Morita semi-contexts** and **Morita data**.

Morita semi-contexts arise in contexts where only a single trace ideal is relevant to the analysis, rather than the pair of trace ideals typically associated with a full Morita context. This simplification is particularly useful in situations where the symmetry between the two rings involved is not preserved or is not the object of study.

Morita data, meanwhile, generalize the classical notion further by relaxing the requirement of compatibility between the bimodule morphisms. In a standard Morita context, the connecting maps must satisfy certain associativity or compatibility conditions relating the two bimodules; Morita data drop this requirement, allowing for a more flexible structure in which the bimodule morphisms can be studied independently. This relaxation broadens the applicability of the theory to settings where such compatibility either fails to hold or is unnecessary for the intended applications.

## Static and Adstatic Modules in the Study of Injective Morita Data

A central technical contribution of the paper is the study of **injective Morita data** through the lens of static and adstatic modules. These module-theoretic tools are employed to establish category equivalences between subcategories of modules that intersect in a specific way—namely, those subcategories associated with localized or colocalized modules relative to the trace ideals of a given Morita datum. By carefully analyzing the interaction between static modules (those for which a certain natural transformation is an isomorphism) and their adstatic counterparts, the authors are able to construct equivalences that generalize the classical Morita equivalence of module categories to this more relaxed setting. This analysis provides a deeper understanding of how partial or asymmetric trace ideal data can still yield meaningful categorical equivalences.

## Application to *-Modules

The theoretical apparatus developed for Morita α-contexts is then applied to the study of ***-modules**, a specific and well-studied class of modules characterized by particular self-duality or reflexivity properties. By situating *-modules within the framework of Morita α-contexts, the paper extends the classical theory of these modules, offering new tools and perspectives for their analysis. This application demonstrates the practical utility of the local projectivity condition central to Morita α-contexts, showing how it naturally accommodates the structural features of *-modules and enriches their theoretical treatment.

## Applications of Injective Right Wide Morita Contexts

Finally, the paper investigates further applications arising from **injective right wide Morita contexts**, a variant of the Morita context framework that incorporates both the injectivity condition and a "wide" structural generalization. This exploration forms part of the broader investigative scope of the paper, illustrating how the various generalized Morita-theoretic frameworks introduced throughout the work interact and can be applied to concrete module-theoretic problems. These applications serve to reinforce the versatility and reach of the theoretical constructions developed in the paper, connecting the abstract categorical framework to specific classes of modules and rings.

## Conclusion

Taken together, these contributions provide a systematic and unified exposition of generalized Morita theory, introducing new conceptual tools—Morita semi-contexts, Morita data, and Morita α-contexts—that extend the classical theory beyond its traditional boundaries. Through the use of static and adstatic module techniques, and through applications to *-modules and wide Morita contexts, the paper demonstrates the richness and flexibility of this generalized framework, opening avenues for further research into non-classical dualities and equivalences in module theory.

# Injective Morita Contexts and Generalized Morita Data: A Study in Localization and Colocalization

## Introduction

Morita theory, since its inception, has provided a fundamental framework for understanding equivalences between module categories over rings. Classical Morita theory establishes that two rings $R$ and $S$ have equivalent module categories if and only if there exists a Morita context $(R, S, {}_RP_S, {}_SQ_R, \tau, \mu)$ satisfying certain surjectivity conditions on the trace maps $\tau: P \otimes_S Q \to R$ and $\mu: Q \otimes_R P \to S$. This classical result has been extended in numerous directions, including partial Morita contexts, Morita contexts with only one-sided surjectivity, and various weakened notions accommodating more general categorical situations.

This paper explores injective Morita contexts and Morita $\alpha$-contexts, situations in which the classical bijectivity or surjectivity conditions on trace maps are relaxed to more subtle injectivity requirements. Such relaxations naturally arise when one wishes to capture partial equivalences—equivalences that hold not on the entire module category, but rather on certain distinguished subcategories determined by torsion-theoretic or localization-theoretic considerations. In many applications, particularly those involving *-modules, tilting modules, or more general classes of modules with prescribed homological properties, only a single trace ideal (rather than a symmetric pair of trace ideals) plays a significant structural role, or the compatibility conditions linking the bimodule morphisms $\tau$ and $\mu$ are weaker than in the classical bijective setting.

To address these phenomena in a unified manner, we introduce two new structural notions: **Morita semi-contexts** and **Morita data**. A Morita semi-context relaxes the classical Morita context by requiring only one of the two trace maps to satisfy the relevant surjectivity or injectivity condition, thereby accommodating asymmetric situations where the bimodules $P$ and $Q$ do not play dual roles. Morita data, on the other hand, generalize this further by relaxing the compatibility conditions between $\tau$ and $\mu$ themselves—specifically, the associativity-type conditions
$$\tau(p \otimes q) p' = p \mu(q \otimes p'), \qquad q\tau(p \otimes q') = \mu(q \otimes p) q'$$
need not hold in full generality, but only up to certain controlled deviations captured by the categorical framework we develop.

## Static and Adstatic Modules

Central to our approach is the use of static and adstatic modules, notions originally introduced in the study of tilting theory and generalized Morita equivalences by Colpi and collaborators. Given a bimodule ${}_RP_S$, a right $S$-module $X$ is said to be **static** (with respect to $P$) if the canonical evaluation morphism
$$\text{Hom}_S(P, X) \otimes_S P \to X$$
wait, more precisely, if the natural map
$$X \to \text{Hom}_R(P, P \otimes_S X)$$
is an isomorphism, appropriately interpreted in the relevant module category. Dually, a left $R$-module $Y$ is called **adstatic** if the corresponding dual evaluation map is an isomorphism. These notions generalize the classical concept of modules for which the unit and counit of a hom-tensor adjunction are isomorphisms, and they play the role that "faithfully balanced" modules play in classical Morita theory.

The subcategories of static and adstatic modules associated to a Morita semi-context or Morita datum are shown to be equivalent via functors induced by $\text{Hom}$ and $\otimes$, though this equivalence in general holds only after restricting to appropriate intersecting subcategories. Specifically, we identify these subcategories as those which are simultaneously **localized** and **colocalized** by the relevant trace ideals: a module $M$ lies in the localized subcategory if the trace ideal action on $M$ is "dense" in an appropriate sense (annihilating a torsion submodule), while colocalization refers to the dual condition on injective hulls or cogenerated submodules.

## Injective Morita Data and Equivalences

The main theorem of this paper establishes that, given an **injective Morita datum**—that is, a Morita datum in which the trace maps $\tau$ and $\mu$ satisfy appropriate injectivity conditions relative to the associated trace ideals $\tau(P \otimes_S Q) \subseteq R$ and $\mu(Q \otimes_R P) \subseteq S$—there is a category equivalence
$$\mathcal{C}_R \simeq \mathcal{C}_S$$
where $\mathcal{C}_R$ and $\mathcal{C}_S$ denote the intersections of the static (resp. adstatic) subcategories with the subcategories of modules localized and colocalized by the respective trace ideals. This equivalence is induced by the functors $P \otimes_S -$ and $Q \otimes_R -$ (or their Hom-theoretic counterparts $\text{Hom}_R(P,-)$ and $\text{Hom}_S(Q,-)$, depending on variance conventions), restricted appropriately.

This result generalizes several known equivalences in the literature, including the classical Morita theorem (recovered when the trace ideals are the entire rings $R$ and $S$), as well as partial equivalences arising in the theory of tilting modules of arbitrary projective dimension, where the trace ideal of the tilting module plays a central structural role.

## Applications

### *-Modules

As a first application, we specialize our general framework to the setting of ***-modules**, a class of modules introduced by Menini and Orsatti and further studied extensively in relation to generalized Morita equivalences. A module ${}_RP$ is a *-module if it induces an equivalence between a torsion class in $\text{Mod-}R$ (or $R\text{-Mod}$) and the category of modules over its endomorphism ring $S = \text{End}(P)$ satisfying appropriate generation conditions. We show that the Morita context naturally associated to a *-module ${}_RP$ (with $Q = P$ and appropriate trace maps) is in fact an injective Morita datum in our sense, and that the equivalence of static and adstatic subcategories recovers, and in some respects strengthens, the classical *-module equivalence theorems. In particular, we clarify the precise relationship between the localized/colocalized subcategories in our framework and the torsion-theoretic subcategories classically associated to *-modules.

### Injective Right Wide Morita Contexts

As a second application, we examine **injective right wide Morita contexts**, a further generalization in which the bimodules $P$ and $Q$ are replaced by families of bimodules indexed by a possibly infinite set, reflecting situations where a single ring $R$ is related to a family of rings $\{S_i\}_{i \in I}$ simultaneously (as arises, for instance, in the study of Morita contexts associated to a family of idempotents, or in the representation theory of certain infinite-dimensional algebras). We show that our machinery of Morita data, static and adstatic modules, and injective conditions extends naturally to this wide setting, yielding equivalences between appropriate intersecting subcategories indexed compatibly across the family $\{S_i\}$. This application illustrates the flexibility of the injective Morita datum framework in handling multi-object and multi-ring generalizations beyond the classical two-ring setting.

## Conclusion

Taken together, these results demonstrate that the notions of Morita semi-contexts, Morita data, and their injective refinements provide a robust and flexible framework for capturing partial Morita-type equivalences arising throughout module theory. By systematically relaxing both the surjectivity conditions on trace maps and the compatibility conditions between bimodule morphisms, and by employing static and adstatic modules to control the resulting equivalences on appropriately localized and colocalized subcategories, we obtain a unified perspective that recovers classical Morita theory, clarifies the structure of *-module equivalences, and extends naturally to wide and multi-ring generalizations. We anticipate that this framework will find further applications in tilting theory, torsion-theoretic module classification, and the study of derived and stable module category equivalences, and we indicate several directions for future research along these lines in our concluding remarks.

# Morita Theory and Its Extensions

This text explores the foundational concept of Morita theory in abstract algebra, along with important contributions made by researchers such as Zimmermann to this rich mathematical field.

## Origins of Morita Theory

Morita theory takes its name from the Japanese mathematician Kiiti Morita, who in the 1950s developed a framework for understanding when two rings have "equivalent" module categories. This equivalence relation, now known as **Morita equivalence**, established that two rings can behave identically from the perspective of module theory even if they are not isomorphic as rings. The central insight was that the category of modules over a ring—rather than the ring itself—often captures the essential algebraic structure relevant to representation theory and homological algebra.

Morita's original theorems characterized precisely when such equivalences exist, typically through the existence of a "progenerator" module that establishes a categorical equivalence via tensor product functors. This became a cornerstone technique for simplifying complex algebraic problems by replacing a given ring with a more tractable, equivalent one.

## Contributions by Zimmermann

Building on this foundation, Wolfgang Zimmermann made significant contributions to the study of **Morita duality**, an extension of Morita's ideas concerned not with equivalences but with dualities between module categories. This research direction investigates when a contravariant functor establishes a duality between the module categories of two rings, generalizing the classical Matlis duality for commutative rings to more general noncommutative settings.

Zimmermann's work, often conducted in collaboration with other algebraists, helped clarify the structural conditions under which such dualities exist, particularly focusing on questions of **self-duality**—situations where a ring is dual to itself. These investigations required deep analysis of injective modules, cogenerators, and linear compactness, connecting Morita's categorical framework to broader questions in ring theory.

## Legacy and Significance

This combination of foundational theory and later refinement illustrates a common pattern in mathematics: an initial breakthrough opens a research program that subsequent scholars extend and deepen. The interplay between Morita's original equivalence theorems and later duality theory, including Zimmermann's contributions, remains an active area of study within noncommutative ring theory, influencing related fields such as representation theory of algebras and the structure theory of Artinian and Noetherian rings.

Together, these developments demonstrate how abstract categorical thinking can unify seemingly disparate algebraic phenomena under a single conceptual umbrella.

# Injective Morita Contexts, Morita α-Contexts, and Applications to *-Modules

**Abstract**

We investigate injective Morita contexts and their generalization, Morita α-contexts, developing a unified framework that connects classical Morita theory with the theory of self-injective modules and quasi-Frobenius rings. A Morita context $(A, B, {}_AM_B, {}_BN_A, \tau, \mu)$ is called *injective* when the connecting bimodule maps satisfy natural nondegeneracy and injectivity conditions ensuring that the associated pairing behaves well with respect to injective envelopes on both sides. We introduce the notion of a Morita α-context, in which the usual bimodule homomorphisms $\tau: M \otimes_B N \to A$ and $\mu: N \otimes_A M \to B$ are relaxed by twisting with a ring automorphism $\alpha$, yielding a broader class of contexts that still preserve much of the categorical machinery of classical Morita equivalence while accommodating twisted and skew module structures.

We establish structural characterizations of injective Morita contexts in terms of the surjectivity and kernel behavior of $\tau$ and $\mu$, and show how these conditions correspond to well-known properties of the module $M$, such as being a generator, a progenerator, or satisfying the double annihilator condition. Building on this, we develop criteria under which the associated rings $A$ and $B$ inherit self-injectivity, and we characterize when the context induces a Morita duality. Particular attention is given to the interaction between injective Morita contexts and *-modules — modules $M$ for which the trace ideal and the associated Morita context give rise to a duality between suitable subcategories of $A$-modules and $B$-modules. We prove that a module $M$ is a *-module precisely when it fits into an injective Morita context satisfying an appropriate closure condition, thereby recovering and extending classical results of Colby–Fuller and Menini–Orsatti within a unified contextual framework.

As applications, we use Morita α-contexts to construct new examples of *-modules over skew group rings, twisted matrix rings, and rings graded by a group with an automorphism action, and we describe how quasi-Frobenius and pseudo-Frobenius rings arise naturally as endomorphism rings of *-modules in this setting. Finally, we discuss how the twisted contexts interact with duality functors $\mathrm{Hom}(-, M)$, yielding new sufficient conditions for a ring to be a QF-ring in terms of the existence of an injective Morita α-context with prescribed properties. These results provide new tools for studying self-duality, linear compactness, and Morita duality in noncommutative ring theory.

# Morita Semi-Contexts, Morita Data, and Category Equivalences: A Structural Analysis

## Abstract

This paper investigates the algebraic architecture underlying Morita theory through a systematic examination of Morita semi-contexts and Morita data as generalized frameworks for establishing equivalences between module categories. Classical Morita theory characterizes equivalences between categories of modules over rings via progenerator bimodules, yet this formulation often obscures the finer bilinear and multiplicative structures that govern such correspondences. We address this gap by formalizing the notion of a Morita semi-context—a quadruple consisting of two rings, an intertwining bimodule pair, and connecting maps satisfying prescribed associativity and unitality constraints—as a foundational structure from which full Morita contexts and their associated equivalences may be systematically constructed or obstructed.

Our approach begins by delineating the precise conditions under which a Morita semi-context extends to a complete Morita context, identifying the surjectivity (or non-surjectivity) of the connecting trace maps as the critical obstruction to inducing a genuine equivalence of module categories. We introduce the concept of Morita data as an enriched categorical packaging of this information, incorporating compatibility conditions with respect to tensor-hom adjunctions and unit/counit morphisms, thereby situating semi-contexts within a broader adjunction-theoretic framework. This perspective allows us to reinterpret the classical Morita theorems not merely as existence statements for equivalences, but as coherence conditions on natural transformations arising from the semi-context data.

We further explore functorial implications: given a Morita semi-context between rings $R$ and $S$, we construct associated functors $R\text{-Mod} \to S\text{-Mod}$ and analyze precisely when these functors fail to be inverse equivalences, characterizing the resulting categories via kernel and cokernel considerations tied to the non-surjective trace ideals. This yields a stratification of "partial Morita equivalences," wherein semi-contexts induce recollement-type relationships or fully faithful embeddings rather than full equivalences, generalizing the dichotomy between Morita equivalence and Morita similarity.

Applications are given to noncommutative ring extensions, corner ring constructions, and comodule categories over corings, where Morita data naturally arise from incomplete or degenerate pairings. We conclude by situating this framework within the broader landscape of categorification and bicategorical Morita theory, suggesting that Morita semi-contexts serve as the appropriate 1-cell data in a bicategory whose 2-cells encode compatible transformations between context maps, thus offering a unifying language for both classical and generalized Morita phenomena across module, comodule, and enriched category settings.

**Keywords:** Morita context, Morita equivalence, module categories, semi-context, tensor-hom adjunction, bicategory, progenerator, recollement

# Abstract

We develop a generalized Morita theory for module categories based on the interplay between trace ideals, static and adstatic modules, and their associated localization and colocalization subcategories. Given a ring homomorphism between two rings, we study the trace ideal of the induced module and show that it governs a pair of subcategories—the static and adstatic modules—which generalize the classical notions arising from Morita contexts and tilting theory. We establish that these subcategories are related by canonical localization and colocalization functors, extending the classical equivalences of Morita theory to a broader, non-equivalence setting.

Our approach unifies several known constructions, including those arising from idempotent ideals, tilting and cotilting modules, and pure-injective envelopes, by placing them within a common framework governed by trace ideal data. We characterize when the induced adjunction restricts to an equivalence between the static and adstatic subcategories, recovering classical Morita equivalence as a special case, and we analyze the obstruction to such an equivalence in terms of the associated trace ideal and its idempotency properties.

Furthermore, we investigate the compatibility of this theory with recollements and torsion pairs, showing that the static and adstatic subcategories fit into a broader categorical landscape connecting representation theory, homological algebra, and the theory of module categories over rings. Applications include new criteria for detecting when finitely generated projective or injective modules induce genuine equivalences of subcategories, as well as a unified treatment of examples from classical ring theory, tilting theory, and covering theory of rings.

This work provides a conceptual and computational framework for understanding partial or "generalized" Morita equivalences, offering new tools for the classification of module categories up to static/adstatic equivalence and clarifying the role of trace ideals as fundamental invariants in this generalized setting.

# Local Projectivity in Morita α-Contexts: A Structural Analysis

## Abstract

This paper investigates the interplay between Zimmermann-Huisgen local projectivity and the module-theoretic structure induced by Morita α-contexts, extending classical bimodule duality theory to a broader categorical framework. A Morita α-context, generalizing the classical Morita context, consists of rings R and S, bimodules ${}_RM_S$ and ${}_SN_R$, together with bimodule homomorphisms $\alpha: M \otimes_S N \to R$ and $\beta: N \otimes_R M \to S$ satisfying a parametrized compatibility condition indexed by α, relaxing the strict associativity constraints of the classical setting. We establish that local projectivity of the connecting bimodules—in the sense of Zimmermann-Huisgen, characterized via the existence of dual bases relative to finite subsets rather than global projectivity—provides a natural sufficient condition under which the induced functors between module categories $\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}R$ and $\mathrm{Mod}\text{-}S$ preserve exactness properties and reflect flatness. We show that when $M_S$ (respectively $N_R$) is locally projective, the maps $\alpha$ and $\beta$ induce a well-behaved adjunction whose unit and counit control the extent to which the associated categories of modules are equivalent, generalizing the classical Morita equivalence criterion to a "near-equivalence" governed by the images of $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Key results include: (i) a characterization of when local projectivity of $M$ over $S$ forces $\alpha$ to be a pure epimorphism; (ii) a Morita-type theorem describing torsion-theoretic invariants preserved under α-context induced functors; (iii) applications to comodule categories over corings and to Galois theory for firm rings, where local projectivity of the underlying bimodules recovers known Galois descent conditions. We further illustrate the theory through examples arising from firm rings, corings without counit, and non-unital ring extensions, demonstrating that the locally projective Morita α-context framework subsumes several known generalizations of classical Morita theory, including those for idempotent rings and s-unital rings. Our results suggest that local projectivity serves as the correct categorical replacement for projectivity in contexts where unitality fails, providing a unifying lens for duality phenomena in non-unital and topological module categories.

**Keywords:** Morita context, local projectivity, firm rings, corings, Galois descent, torsion theory

# Abstract

Let $R$ and $S$ be rings connected by a Morita context $(R, S, {}_RM_S, {}_SN_R, \phi, \psi)$. In this paper, we investigate a generalized framework, termed *injective wide Morita contexts*, in which the connecting bimodules $M$ and $N$ need not induce a genuine equivalence but instead satisfy suitable injectivity and compatibility conditions with respect to the pairings $\phi: M \otimes_S N \to R$ and $\psi: N \otimes_R M \to S$. We study the structural properties of such contexts, focusing on the interplay between the injectivity hypotheses and the exactness behavior of the associated Hom and tensor functors.

A central theme of the paper is the relationship between injective wide Morita contexts and the theory of *-modules, introduced originally to study tilting-type dualities and faithfully balanced bimodules. We show that a wide Morita context is injective precisely when the module $M$ (respectively $N$) satisfies a *-module condition relative to the context maps, thereby situating classical *-module theory within the broader categorical setting of Morita-type correspondences. This connection allows us to transfer duality results for *-modules into statements about the surjectivity or injectivity of the trace ideals $\mathrm{Im}(\phi)$ and $\mathrm{Im}(\psi)$, and conversely to derive new examples of *-modules from wide Morita contexts arising naturally in ring extensions, idealizer constructions, and endomorphism rings of injective or projective modules.

We further examine the associated *Morita data*—consisting of the induced adjoint pairs of functors between module categories together with their unit and counit natural transformations—and characterize when these data define a full Morita equivalence, a one-sided equivalence, or merely a torsion-theoretic correspondence between subcategories of $R$-Mod and $S$-Mod. Necessary and sufficient conditions are given, in terms of the injectivity of $M_S$ and $N_R$ and the surjectivity of the trace maps, for the induced adjunctions to restrict to equivalences on the categories of modules that are "static" or "adstatic" with respect to the context. Several illustrative examples are provided, including contexts arising from corner rings $eRe$, from module categories over triangular matrix rings, and from generalized matrix rings associated to bimodules with one-sided perfect duality.

Our results unify and extend earlier work on Morita contexts without the equivalence assumption, clarify the precise sense in which *-modules generate injective wide Morita contexts, and provide new tools for constructing dualities between subcategories of modules over non-Morita-equivalent rings.
